touches.text: scratch: a proof's throwaway temp dirs and worktrees, cleaned up by the door. WHY: a run must leave nothing behind (4.3.1.7). USERS: the tester.
It outputs only its findings. It certifies nothing, records no crossing, and posts nothing; the gate consumes its findings.

Once build_inspector moves into CodeMother, code outside her reaches it over the bus: the 18 crossing calls in transitions.py, the other code sites and the 82 proofs that run a sieve over themselves. No published client tool, no fifth exception. Akien 2026-11-13, on Q#88: "over the bus. that's what it's for?"

A rule not yet enforced is made into a ticket now. Akien 2026-11-13, on Q#89: "i said no ious because you were making a lot of them. ious have to be made into tickets. if we have them floating around, then they need to be made tickets NOW." So ticket f5dbfddea8c6 makes the rewrites it proposed at the 24 remaining sites (CLAUDE.md, MAP.md, the press office, PROOF.md). Where a site names a rule whose physics is not built, it names that rule's real ticket id, cast now if none exists; the word "ticket" with no id behind it does not count. CC's reading of his answer, on a mechanism CC made.

Commit: the proofs of the component the ticket changed, since RULE 1 bounds a change to its component. Passing them puts the component in service, yellow: proven where it changed, not yet measured against what depends on it. Akien: "being put in service only requires that it's the best we can do now. only requires 80% trust."

A seal is host independent: one record per proof, whichever box asks. Seals are made by one sealing machine in the cairn device, and there is only ever one cairn (until a laptop dies and a backup takes over), so there is one sealer. A box that is not cairn's home asks the sealer instead of writing its own seal. Akien 2026-11-13, answering Q#90 (a Windows reseal of a mixed proof overwrote the Linux seal, measured 2026-11-12): "then we have to invent a way for seals to be host independent. one way would be to create a sealing machine in cairn. there's only ever one cairn until we have a laptop die and have to fail over to a backup".

Every sieve carries its own why, and the why names where it came from. Akien designed the inspector tools; CC built each specific sieve from what it read him to mean. So the adjudication in 17.11.6 is against the sieve's own why, done by CC, and never a question to him. Akien 2026-11-13: "I designed the tools, but not the specific sieves. you built those to handle what you thought i meant for each inspector. ... i don't know why each sieve is there. we are supposed to add a why to each sieve so we can help adjudicate it. and this is also why the sieves are not perfect. Nothing in this system ever will be perfect. the whole thing will constantly be under improvement." Measured that day: build_inspector registers 43 sieves, and the 36 sieves/*.json records carry name, band and dials but no why. The whys live only in docstrings.

The same boundary runs wherever Akien designed a tool or machine and CC filled in its specific contents: the nest and its questions, the inspectors and their sieves, the gates and their checks, the corrosion set, the skill doors and their field lists. Each such component's charter carries a design_boundary naming what Akien designed, what CC designed, and how a red over CC's part is settled. CC's part is CC's to adjudicate against its own why. Akien may be asked whether a part could be better, with the whys laid out, and whatever CC can't sort goes to him. A new component that has this boundary declares it in its charter when it is born. Akien 2026-11-13: "i think we make a note in the nest and/or sieve tools/machines that the specific contents are at your design. and anywhere else we wind up with an akien/claude boundary. because i'm aware I hadn't thought about that boundary until today."
A sieve's rule follows the ticket's kind, read off the ticket, so it stays deterministic; 17.11.6 is left for what the rules do not cover.

Lifetimes. Each tree declares its lifetime when it is made: kept, one activity (eg one sleep run), or until its source file changes. Dropping a tree drops its leaves and its own links. A node goes only when no tree indexes it, so whatever a temporary tree's activity promoted into a permanent tree outlives it. The drop is enforced, not a habit. WHY: a run that ends without dropping its tables leaves them behind forever.
